source_read: PDF (scan), pp. 233-241, all pages read on the rendered page at 150 dpi; pp. 235-239 at 300 dpi; Tables 1-2 and the blood-alcohol line on p. 239 at 600-1200 dpi; text layer used only to locate passages

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of this source in substance. Three wording points: (1) 'so a moderate effect cannot be ruled out' needs a direction: the interval for the beverage effect (-5.8 to +2.8 oz, about -0.68 to +0.33 SD) rules out an increase larger than about a third of an SD across both groups, while a moderate decrease cannot be ruled out; within the 16 men with alcohol problems alone (cells of 8) the same calculation gives about -7.2 to +4.8 oz, so a moderate increase in that group is not excluded. (2) '8 men per condition' is not printed; it follows from 32 per group randomly assigned to four cells and fits the error df of 56; it is 8 per cell (group x condition), 16 per condition across both groups. (3) The per-3-minute drinking pattern is the authors' approximation (amount per sip times sips in each block), not measured amounts.
claims.note: Every number from this source in the statement and magnitude was checked on the rendered page and matches. Recomputed: told-vodka mean (23.00 + 14.53)/2 = 18.77 oz (the text's 17.77 is a misprint against Table 1; told tonic (10.60 + 7.63)/2 = 9.12); ratio 2.06. d from F = 20.59 with 32 per level: 4.538 x sqrt(2/32) = 1.13. Interval: I get 0.63 to 1.64 only when the SD is treated as known (raw difference 9.65 oz, 95% CI 5.39 to 13.92, divided by the pooled within-cell SD 8.51); the noncentral-t (or Hedges-Olkin) interval is 0.60 to 1.66, so '0.6 to 1.7' would be the exact rounding. Beverage effect: 13.19 - 14.69 = -1.50 oz, SE 2.13 (same MSE 72.4, which the beverage F = .50 also implies), 95% CI -5.76 to +2.77: matches. Cell means match Table 1 exactly. Blood alcohol: the four estimated means on p. 239 are .093% and .056% (men with alcohol problems, told vodka and told tonic) and .044% and .031% (social drinkers); the .056 is partly under a pen mark (OCR reads .055), irrelevant to the .031-.093 range; these apply only to men given vodka and were calculated from body weight and alcohol consumed with a 1959 AMA formula. Internal inconsistency: p. 239 says the alcoholic group was on average 6 years older, but the means on p. 235 differ by 9.56 years. Other context the claim need not carry: alcoholic group drank more overall (16.80 vs 11.08 oz, F = 7.22, p < .01); group x set and set x beverage interactions not significant (three-way not reported); sip frequency was not changed by set but was lower when given vodka (22.25 vs 29.16, F = 4.01, p < .05); post-task estimates of alcohol content followed set only (1% vs 27.6%, F = 44.49), told vodka/given tonic estimating more (28.7%, 37.2%) than told vodka/given vodka (21.3%, 23.1%). The experimenter who mixed the drinks knew the condition; the observer behind the mirror did not. Volunteer sample recruited through hotels, bars, an ex-patient and a newspaper ad, paid $5.

anchors.locator: Method > Subjects > Alcoholic group (right column, last paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Attempt to recruit 32 men with alcoholism aged 21-65 who were currently not abstinent, from in and around Madison, Wisconsin: sign-up sheets with hotel desk clerks and bartenders, names gathered by a former patient, and friends of subjects. Placebo selection (same column): 25 student social drinkers could not tell a 5:1 tonic-to-vodka mix from tonic better than chance (44% said alcohol, 56% none).

anchors.locator: Method > Subjects (left column, 2nd-3rd paragraphs; right column, Control group and 2nd paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Alcoholic group: one or more of at least one admission to an alcoholism treatment centre, five or more drunk-and-disorderly arrests, or past membership of AA or the local Vocational Rehabilitation for Alcoholics Program; all but 7 of 32 met two or more; 23 treated (mean 5.5 admissions), 21 arrested (mean 21.5 arrests), 18 AA, 10 rehabilitation programme; all had drunk within the prior 2 weeks with no immediate intention to abstain. Breathalyser above .06% sent home; weighed and randomly assigned. Controls: 32 male social drinkers, excluded if they reported heavy or problem drinking. Ages 24-65 (mean 46.75) vs 23-63 (mean 37.19), difference p < .01; social class index 59.2 vs 52.2 (both class IV).

anchors.locator: Procedure > Treatment conditions; Primer dose; Task procedure
anchors.extracted: Each group randomly assigned to the four cells of told vodka-and-tonic or tonic x given vodka-and-tonic (5:1) or tonic, so 8 per cell (derived; error df 56). Study conditions: a primer of three 2-oz samples (1 oz of 80-proof vodka in total, or tonic) about 20 min before; 72 oz available in three decanters; mouthwash with added alcohol; 15-minute taste-rating task of unannounced length; observer behind a one-way mirror unaware of condition; the experimenter mixed drinks in front of the subject.

anchors.locator: Results > Amount of Beverage Consumed; Table 1
anchors.extracted: 2 x 2 x 2 fixed-effects ANOVA. Instructional set F = 20.59, df 1/56, p < .01: told tonic 9.12 oz, told vodka 17.77 oz in the text (Table 1 margins give 18.77). Actual beverage F = .50, df 1/56: given tonic 14.69, given vodka 13.19 (grand mean 13.94); set x beverage not significant. Group: 16.80 vs 11.08 oz, F = 7.22, p < .01; group x set not significant. Cells (given tonic / given vodka): alcoholic group told tonic 10.94 / 10.25, told vodka 23.87 / 22.13; social drinkers told tonic 9.31 / 5.94, told vodka 14.62 / 14.44.

anchors.locator: Results > Sip Rate, Table 2; Amount Consumed Per Sip, Table 3
anchors.extracted: Sip frequency: group F = 5.68, p < .025 (controls 29.81, alcoholic group 21.59) and beverage F = 4.01, p < .05 (given tonic 29.16, given vodka 22.25); set not significant (Table 2 margins 25.9 told tonic vs 25.5 told vodka). Amount per sip: set F = 11.89, p < .01 (.94 vs .46 oz); group F = 10.65, p < .01 (.92 vs .48); beverage not significant.

anchors.locator: Figure 1 (p. 238) and Results text (p. 239, left column, 1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Per-3-minute amounts are approximations (amount per sip times sips). Highest consumption in the first 3-minute block, falling over the next 12 minutes in most groups; exception: social drinkers told tonic/given vodka, stable and low. On the figure, the alcoholic group told tonic/given vodka peaks in the second block and told vodka/given vodka rises slightly in the last block (about 2 to 3 oz).

anchors.locator: Results > Estimates of Alcohol Content; Table 4
anchors.extracted: Only set affected post-task estimates of alcohol content (F = 44.49, df 1/56, p < .01): 1% told tonic vs 27.6% told vodka; told vodka/given vodka 21.3% and 23.1%, told vodka/given tonic 28.7% and 37.2%, told tonic/given vodka 0% and 3.5% (alcoholic group, controls).

anchors.locator: Results > Postexperimental Blood-Alcohol Concentrations (left column end; right column, 1st-2nd paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: Estimated (formula from weight and alcohol consumed), for men given vodka only: alcoholic group .093% told vodka and .056% told tonic; controls .044% and .031%. Age not significantly correlated with any consumption measure; the text calls the age gap 6 years although the means differ by 9.56.

anchors.locator: Discussion (p. 240 right column, 2nd paragraph; p. 241 left column, 1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Loss of control, as progressive increase in drinking among men given alcohol, was not shown; rates decreased over the task, possibly because of task demands. Authors list limits: task perhaps too short, blood alcohol perhaps below the level at which loss of control appears, taste-test demand characteristics; generalisation to natural drinking settings must be examined.

key_findings.correction: Finding, numbers and location confirmed (18.77 from Table 1 and 18.76 from the grand mean both reproduce). The editors' interval 0.63 to 1.64 treats the SD as known; the noncentral-t interval for d = 1.13 (t = 4.54, df 56) is 0.60 to 1.66. Consider giving that, or labelling the method.
Reproduced: -1.5 oz (-5.76 to +2.77), d -0.18; within the alcoholism group -1.2 oz (-7.2 to +4.8). The noncentral-t interval for d is -0.67 to +0.32 (card: -0.68 to 0.33), a trivial difference.
Editors' interaction estimate reproduced (contrast 5.5 oz, F(1,56) = 1.67, p = .20).
I also read the partly obscured value as .056 on a 1200-dpi crop.
My independent reading of Figure 1 agrees (alcoholism group told and given alcohol about 7.9, 6.0, 4.4, 2.0, 2.9 oz).

Content confirmed. The point that participants may have cut down because intoxication would hurt their ratings (or to please the experimenter) is in the Discussion's 4th paragraph (p. 240, right column, the paragraph on loss of control), not the 3rd. The 3rd paragraph, which runs onto the right column, is the taste-discrimination alternative. The 5th-6th paragraph locators are right. Suggested locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 240, right column) and 5th-6th paragraphs (pp. 240-241).

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in the blind reading (9.56 years on the printed means).
p. 236 (primer of 2 oz from each of the three drinks) and p. 237 (amount computed from 72 oz allowing for the 6-oz primer; Results say up to 72 oz were available during the task).
Implied within-cell SDs reproduced: 8.51 (instructions F), 8.46 (beverage F), 8.52 (group F).

The per-ounce arithmetic is right (.0042, .0055, .0030, .0052). But cells of 8 men differ in body weight, and a fixed amount of alcohol from the primer would also do this if the formula counted it (the paper says it used alcohol drunk in the task). Either would give the higher per-ounce values seen in the two cells that drank less (told tonic). So the lack of proportion means the estimates cannot be checked; it does not show an error.
Same two rises seen in the blind reading of Figure 1.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 some concerns overall, with the domain judgments as given. The experimenter's knowledge of the assignment is built into the deception (drinks mixed in front of the participant), and the volume outcome is objective, so the main expectancy effect is credible within the task.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The authors themselves name the limits that bound the claim (short task, low blood alcohol, taste-test demand). The unprinted simple-effect claim about the alcoholism group is correctly flagged. My reproduction of the editors' test is t(56) = 2.81, p = .007.

missed: p. 240, Discussion 3rd paragraph (left column end, continuing at the top of the right column): the authors say their data do not rule out a task explanation for the main finding. Men told the drinks held vodka may have sampled more because detecting vodka in a mixed drink is harder than judging tonic, which is a taste-discrimination effect rather than an expected-reinforcement effect. They argue against it because the alcoholism group drank more than social drinkers in the told-vodka cells, and because social drinkers sipped more often. Relevant data the card already has: the instructions did not change sip frequency (Table 2) but nearly doubled the amount per sip (Table 3), which fits larger gulps better than more tasting. Worth a key finding or a line in the interpretation gap, since it bears on what the expectancy effect means.
